articles.title: Content escalation, content homogenization, and user immersion: a three-dimensional conceptualization of online rabbit holes
articles.authors: Ine Beyens, Qiru Huo, Konrad Mikalauskas, Rebecca Godard, Amber van der Wal
articles.abstract: Online environments are often described as drawing users into a “rabbit hole.” While the term is frequently invoked in both academic and popular discourse, there is little consensus on what precisely constitutes an online rabbit hole. This lack of consensus has resulted in research on this phenomenon being conceptually fragmented and inconsistent. The current scoping review addresses this gap by systematically examining how online rabbit holes have been conceptualized and operationalized. Through a critical synthesis of 30 studies, we derive three recurring dimensions in the different conceptualizations of the online rabbit hole: content escalation, content homogenization, and user immersion. Building on these three key dimensions, we propose a comprehensive three-dimensional conceptual framework for understanding online rabbit holes and offer recommendations for accurately measuring and detecting them.

articles.title: ‘Flirting’ with the audience: Broadway Cinematheque’s participation, play, and affective economics on Threads
articles.authors: Hannah Poon
articles.abstract: This article presents Broadway Cinematheque, Hong Kong’s arthouse cinema, as a case study of a brand-participatory affective economics enabled by social media. Since the launch of Threads in 2023, Broadway Cinematheque has become an active participant in the local online film network with its cinephile-like persona and witty promotional strategies. Meanwhile, audiences frequently reference the cinema or appropriate its content for self-expression and play. Focussing on their engagement practices and the platform mediality of Threads, this article argues that Broadway Cinematheque does not simply exploit audiences but ‘flirts’ with them in intimate, playful, and performative ways. By delineating four forms of ‘flirting’ between the cinema and its audiences – participatory intimacy, nostalgic appropriation, myth-making play, and ironic self-roasting, it formulates ‘flirting’ as a highly networked, participatory, and contingent mode of engagement embedded in the platform mediality of Threads. Because of this contingency, it has the potential to open up ways of meaning making and affective patterning of the audience that redistribute, overspill, or destabilise the cinema’s economics.

articles.title: Unfinished becoming: Seriality, temporality, and the making of literature on Wenxuecity
articles.authors: Shaohua Guo
articles.abstract: This article examines Wenxuecity, a long-running website for overseas Chinese communities, as a site of diasporic literary production shaped by distinctive temporal practices. Drawing on the serialized fiction of two active contributors and sustained observation of forum discussions, it identifies three intertwined temporalities: narrative, processual, and archival. Narrative temporality foregrounds authors’ self-directed rhythms of storytelling; processual temporality traces how ongoing exchanges between authors and readers turn writing into a collective, open-ended practice; and archival temporality reveals how dispersed texts accumulate into a layered record of diasporic becoming. The article argues that these temporal practices sustain a mode of digital cultural production oriented toward continuity, participation, and lived experience—one that contests the extractive logics of platform economies rather than merely operating within them. As a fragile media archive, Wenxuecity holds cultural memory in the constitutive tension between accumulation and precarity.

articles.title: “Gender essentialism is cringe”: Brazilian and Ukrainian queer players’ strategies for queering character interactions
articles.authors: Mark Maletska, Thais Arrias Weiller
articles.abstract: This article presents the strategies that Brazilian transgender and gender diverse (TGD) players use to queer character interactions and accommodate diverse gender identities into video games, and aims to show the differences in queering strategies between Brazilian and Ukrainian players. Reflexive thematic analysis was used on survey data gathered from Brazilian and Ukrainian players. The main finding reveals the strategies for queering character interactions distinguished in Brazilian players’ responses, namely, (1) playing with an idealised self, (2) queering binary player characters, and (3) rejecting non-queerness. The results show similar ways of approaching gender binaries and treating them as queer (able), with coinciding reasoning behind. Brazilian respondents also reflected on the significance of player characters as “additional” or “alternative” bodies to experiment with, which differed from Ukrainian players seeking queerness while doubting the potential of video game spaces to accommodate their identities. The results highlight the need for further culturally informed and geographically diverse research on TGD players’ experiences in video games. The findings reflect a similar approach to gender binaries in Brazilian and Ukrainian TGD players’ experience that differs from previous research. It is also shown how bodily focused Brazilian culture makes their experiences more focused on in-game bodies.

articles.title: AI for the audiences: Envisioning the future media environment
articles.authors: Henrik Rydenfelt, Joel Kiskola, Thomas Olsson
articles.abstract: The rapid development and broad-ranging deployment of generative AI poses significant repercussions for media and journalism. Media research has primarily concentrated on newsroom applications, while the potential use of AI by audiences remains underexplored. Drawing on theoretical lenses from media and communication studies, we examine how generative AI in media consumption may drive a shift in the media and information environment. Our empirical study with 17 researcher participants employs design fictions to explore this shift. We analyse and discuss the envisioned development in terms of potential changes in media consumption, audience relationship and key information concerns, with implications for media processes and journalist roles, audience agency, media business models and societal engagement.

articles.title: Prospective Associations Between Emotion Dysregulation, Problematic Internet Use, Internalizing Symptoms, and Life Satisfaction: A Baseline-Adjusted Two-Wave Study of Polish Adults
articles.authors: Paweł Holas, Patryk Roczon
articles.abstract: Longitudinal evidence remains limited on whether the association between problematic Internet use (PIU) and life satisfaction persists after accounting for prior PIU, internalizing symptoms, and life satisfaction. This study examined whether baseline emotion regulation difficulties prospectively predicted PIU, depressive and generalized anxiety symptoms, and life satisfaction 6 months later. Participants were 2,122 Polish adults aged 19–98 years; 1,412 completed follow-up. All constructs were assessed at both waves. Baseline-adjusted path models used 50 multiply imputed datasets. Baseline emotion dysregulation predicted higher PIU ( β = 0.155, 95 percent confidence interval [CI] [0.107, 0.204], p < 0.001) and internalizing symptoms at follow-up. Within T2, PIU was positively associated with internalizing symptoms, which were negatively associated with life satisfaction; direct PIU–life satisfaction paths were negligible (depressive symptoms: β = 0.004, 95 percent CI [−0.035, 0.042], p = 0.846; generalized anxiety symptoms: β = 0.002, 95 percent CI [−0.037, 0.041], p = 0.926). The serial indirect associations were statistically significant but very small: depressive symptoms, β = −0.004, 95 percent CI [−0.006, −0.002], p < 0.001; generalized anxiety symptoms, β = −0.004, 95 percent CI [−0.006, −0.001], p = 0.002. Reciprocal prospective sensitivity models showed small PIU-to-symptom associations but no prospective PIU-to-life-satisfaction association. Other sensitivity analyses did not materially alter the findings. The findings highlight the contribution of internalizing symptoms to the PIU–life satisfaction association after baseline adjustment, but same-wave indirect pathways do not establish temporal mediation or intervention benefits.

articles.title: Procedural Feminism Through Game Design: Towards an Analytical Framework for Situating Games as Feminist Artefacts
articles.authors: Neema Iyer
articles.abstract: Digital games are increasingly recognised as cultural artefacts that encode worldviews, power and possibilities through play. However, dominant frameworks for game analysis do not sufficiently account for power, epistemology and labour, limiting feminist critique to representation alone. This paper proposes the SPIRAL framework (Situated Production, Identity, Rules, Agency and Labour) as a feminist analytic intervention, extending beyond existing frameworks in some dimensions and reworking their categories in others, organising game analysis around epistemology, care and embodied practice to make visible how power is organised procedurally through play. Grounded in feminist technoscience, affect theory, decolonial feminism and procedural feminism, the framework is demonstrated through close readings of Mutazione , Flower and Stardew Valley . Comparative analysis then shows how feminist potential emerges relationally along dimensions. SPIRAL offers a framework for designers and scholars to guide both the development and evaluation of how games shape power and relations through systems.

articles.title: Narrative character networks are associated with storytelling success
articles.authors: Xuanjun Gong, Allison Eden, Frederic R Hopp, Anna W Wolfe, Matthew Grizzard
articles.abstract: Narratives are central to human communication and entertainment, yet why some stories captivate audiences better than others remains poorly understood. Building on theories emphasizing character interdependence, this study introduces a network-based framework for examining storytelling success. We conceptualize narratives as networks composed of characters and their interactions and apply large-scale computational analysis to over 10,000 novels and 1,000 film screenplays. Structural features of these networks are related to storytelling success: lower clustering is associated with greater novel popularity and higher film ratings, whereas higher modularity is associated only with novel popularity and shorter path lengths only with film ratings. These findings demonstrate that storytelling success is related to how characters are structurally connected and organized. By formalizing story architecture as a measurable network, we provide a scalable framework for advancing media entertainment theory, linking cognitive models of graph learning with the structural organization of stories at scale.

articles.title: Does transparency matter when interacting with social bots? An experiment on user engagement behaviors in Chinese social media
articles.authors: Hao Xu, Shaobo Liang, Qingxuan Cheng
articles.abstract: Purpose While transparency is widely promoted as a principle of responsible AI design, its behavioral consequences remain contested, particularly in Chinese social media contexts. This study examines whether different levels of social bot transparency reduce or facilitate user engagement, and whether these effects depend on users' prior knowledge of social bots. Design/methodology/approach An online experiment was conducted in a simulated Weibo environment. A total of 731 participants were randomly assigned to one of three transparency conditions: low, medium, or high transparency. User engagement behaviors were measured through participants' behavioral choices, including reading, liking/sharing, replying, and combined engagement actions. Multinomial logistic regression and subgroup analyses were used to examine the effects of transparency and the moderating role of prior knowledge. Findings Social bot transparency significantly reduces active user engagement. Compared with high transparency, low transparency increases the likelihood of liking/sharing, replying, and combined reply-based engagement rather than merely reading. Medium transparency produces engagement patterns similar to high transparency, suggesting that even ambiguous bot identity cues may activate non-human attribution and suppress active engagement. Prior knowledge moderates this relationship: users with limited prior knowledge are more sensitive to transparency cues, whereas those with higher prior knowledge show more stable engagement across transparency conditions. Originality/value This study extends social bot transparency research beyond binary disclosure by identifying a categorical identity-attribution mechanism. It also clarifies prior knowledge as a boundary condition of algorithm aversion in human-AI interaction.

articles.title: Beyond Human–AI interaction: exploring the influence of AI anthropomorphism on work engagement
articles.authors: Bin Ling, Yuting Xia, Yujie Cai
articles.abstract: Purpose This study examines how anthropomorphic cues that make AI agency socially salient influence employee work engagement in mandatory, performance-oriented human–AI collaboration. It distinguishes AI agency from AI anthropomorphism, tests affective and evaluative motivational mechanisms and identifies perceived AI threat as a boundary condition grounded in the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model. Design/methodology/approach Across two pilot studies and two main experiments (total N = 501), we used immersive workplace role-playing scenarios to test a dual-pathway model. Integrating social response theory with the JD-R model, this research tests a dual-pathway model in which anthropomorphic design influences work engagement through emotional bonding and acquisitive impression management motive (IMM), whereas perceived artificial intelligence threat operates as a hindrance demand that weakens these resource pathways. Findings Anthropomorphic AI enhanced work engagement through two motivational routes: an affective route via emotional bonding and an evaluative route via IMM. However, perceived AI threat significantly attenuated these benefits. When threat was high, the positive effects of anthropomorphism on emotional bonding, IMM and work engagement became non-significant, suggesting that replacement-related threat drains the psychological capacity needed for anthropomorphic cues to function as job resources. Originality/value This research contributes to workplace AI and information systems (IS) scholarship by clarifying how anthropomorphic cues make AI agency socially salient without equating anthropomorphism with agency. It extends prior work on anthropomorphic AI and engagement by identifying an evaluative pathway – performing for AI – alongside the affective pathway of bonding with AI. It also offers a contingency-based explanation for the anthropomorphism paradox by showing that the benefits of humanlike design depend on the surrounding AI-threat climate.

articles.title: Human-in-the-Loop AI for resilient supply chain operations: a framework for augmented decision-making and ethical deployment
articles.authors: Mehtab Alam, Chandra Kanta Samal, Shamsh Parveen, Ashraf Ali, Abdullah Alourani
articles.abstract: Purpose This research examines how Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) artificial intelligence (AI) can support resilient decision-making, operational performance, transparency, trust and ethical accountability in operations and supply chain management (OSCM). Design/methodology/approach The research adopts a design science research approach combined with comparative case analysis. A HITL AI framework, termed the adaptive oversight architecture (AOA), was developed and evaluated in two contrasting OSCM contexts. System logs, operational observations, interviews and performance indicators were analysed to examine decision outcomes, human oversight, trust and accountability. Findings HITL integration was associated with improved exception-handling accuracy, reduced human override frequency, shorter task-completion times and higher user satisfaction across the two cases. Qualitative findings further indicate that trust calibration, training, interface design, workflow integration and organizational governance influence how effectively human oversight operates. The findings also identify risks of automation dependence, accountability diffusion and inappropriate reliance on algorithmic recommendations. Research limitations/implications The research is limited to two case firms, which constrains the generalizability of the findings. While the dual-case approach provides in-depth insights, broader studies involving larger datasets or cross-industry comparisons are needed to validate the proposed framework. Future research could extend the empirical base by employing longitudinal analysis, simulations or hybrid models that test HITL effectiveness under different operational conditions. These directions will allow for a more comprehensive understanding of the scalability, adaptability and long-term organizational impacts of HITL-enabled supply chains. Practical implications For practitioners, the research highlights how HITL can be implemented to strengthen supply chain decision-making while ensuring compliance with ethical and regulatory standards. It suggests that organizations should prioritize training programs, design user-friendly interfaces and establish override mechanisms to maximize HITL effectiveness. The findings emphasize the importance of aligning AI investments with human oversight structures, rather than pursuing automation in isolation. Managers can use the framework to evaluate readiness, map decision tasks suitable for HITL integration and design workflows that balance speed, transparency and accountability. Social implications By positioning humans as active collaborators, HITL contributes to responsible AI adoption that safeguards jobs, reinforces accountability and reduces risks of algorithmic bias in supply chain operations. The approach ensures that technology complements rather than replaces human expertise, fostering inclusive digital transformation. From a societal perspective, embedding ethical safeguards into AI decision-making promotes trust in enterprise systems and enhances their legitimacy. The findings encourage the development of AI solutions that not only drive operational efficiency but also align with broader social values of fairness, responsibility and human dignity. Originality/value This research conceptualizes HITL as a dynamic socio-technical arrangement rather than a static control mechanism. The proposed AOA explains how human authority, algorithmic decision-making and organizational governance interact through oversight, trust calibration and distributed accountability, providing a mechanism-based conceptualization of HITL for OSCM.

articles.title: Social bots as companions: Boon or bane for mental health community engagement?
articles.authors: Shuang Geng, Huimei Tao, Yuanyue Feng, Zhao Du, Ben Niu
articles.abstract: Purpose As AI-powered social bots are increasingly used as companions in mental health communities, their impact on human-to-human interactions remains unclear. This study examines how social bots' replies shape users' subsequent replying behavior and investigates the underlying psychological mechanisms behind users' perception of companionship. Design/methodology/approach This study adopted a multi-method research design comprising two studies. Study 1 examined whether social bot responses were associated with subsequent engagement of posting users and other community members by comparing posts that received social bot responses with posts that received only human responses. Study 2 examined the underlying mechanisms by investigating how users perceive responses from humans and from social bots, respectively, through an online experiment. Findings Posts receiving social bots' responses were associated with faster replies but lower subsequent reply frequency from original posters. They were also associated with fewer human repliers, fewer human replies and lower average replies per user. Human responses outperformed social bots' responses in terms of perceived companionship. The difference was explained by higher perceived psychological closeness, perceived authenticity and empathy. Research limitations/implications Although social bots may accelerate human responses, they cannot replicate the psychological depth of human connection. Platforms should therefore deploy social bots cautiously as supplementary companionship resources in virtual mental health communities. Originality/value This study contributes to an understanding of how social bots' replies reshape community engagement in virtual mental health communities. It also reveals the psychological mechanisms underlying users' different perceptions of human users and AI-powered social bots.

articles.title: GenAI-enabled algorithmic control and gig workers' continuance work intention: evidence from ride-hailing drivers
articles.authors: Peng Wang, Congying Jiang, Xueyan Dong, Tianhui Gao, Lin Zhang
articles.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study is to examine how perceived GenAI-enabled algorithmic control influences ride-hailing drivers' continuance work intention and to unpack the underlying mechanisms from a double-edged sword perspective by testing the mediating role of challenge and hindrance stress and the moderating role of family motivation. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the cognitive appraisal theory of stress and self-determination theory, this study develops and tests a theoretical model using online survey data from 514 ride-hailing drivers in China. The research model is tested using structural equation modeling (SEM). Findings The results showed that GenAI-enabled standardized guidance and GenAI-enabled behavioral constraints elicited both challenge and hindrance stress, whereas GenAI-enabled tracking evaluation elicited only hindrance stress. Hindrance stress increased drivers' withdrawal intention but had no significant effect on continuance intention, whereas challenge stress increased continuance intention but had no significant effect on withdrawal intention. Family motivation positively moderated the effects of both hindrance and challenge stress on continuance intention. Practical implications This study offers significant practical implications for ride-hailing platforms. Importantly, when deploying GenAI-enabled algorithms, platforms should strike a balance between standardization and humanization while continuing to promote efficiency-enhancing tools. Originality/value This research extends the GenAI literature by deepening the understanding of GenAI-enabled algorithmic control within the labor process. Furthermore, this study examines how family motivation moderates these relationships, offering a more nuanced view of ride-hailing drivers' work intentions in the digital age.

articles.title: Revealing the restrictiveness-fairness paradox in general data protection regulation consent practices: evidence from a mixed-methods study
articles.authors: Yasser Al Helaly, Afshin Ashofteh
articles.abstract: Purpose Restrictive cookie consent may satisfy regulatory requirements while limiting meaningful privacy choice. Existing privacy research explains why users disclose information despite privacy concerns, but less is known about why they continue using digital services after judging consent procedures as unfair. This study examines how users interpret restrictive consent, how regulatory contexts shape evaluations and why unfairness coexists with continued engagement. Design/methodology/approach An exploratory sequential mixed-methods design was used. Study 1 analyzed qualitative responses from users in General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and non-GDPR contexts to develop a Communication Privacy Management (CPM)-based model. Study 2 tested the model through two experiments and a pooled post hoc analysis examining how restrictiveness and institutional privacy boundaries shape privacy risk-control assessments, fairness and intention to use online flight-booking websites. Findings Restrictive consent consistently reduced perceived fairness without reliably reducing intention to use website services, revealing a Restrictiveness-Fairness Paradox: users continue engaging despite judging consent procedures as unfair. GDPR also functions as an institutional privacy boundary that changes the fairness cues users rely on. Research limitations/implications The study identifies procedural fairness as a distinct mechanism underlying continued engagement and extends CPM theory by conceptualizing restrictive consent as privacy turbulence and GDPR as an institutional privacy boundary. Practical implications Legal compliance alone may not ensure perceived fairness. The study introduces Fairness Calibration, whereby organizations align consent interfaces with users’ fairness expectations and institutional context to support meaningful choice. Social implications The findings suggest that meaningful consent and perceived fairness are important for trust in digital services, particularly across uneven regulatory contexts, supporting more transparent and user-centered privacy protections. Originality/value The study conceptualizes the Restrictiveness-Fairness Paradox as a distinct form of behavioral persistence under constrained privacy choice.

articles.title: When it’s your own child: effects of media narratives on U.S. parents’ support for their LGBTQ+ teen
articles.authors: Marie-Louise Mares, Y Anthony Chen
articles.abstract: Parents’ responses to their LGBTQ+ child are varied, often intense, and have important consequences for the child. To examine how media depictions may shape responses, a pre-registered online experiment of 494 parents tested effects of viewing two TV narratives, depicting either control (non-LGBTQ+) family interactions, parental rejection, gradual growth toward acceptance, or unalloyed acceptance, of a lesbian or transgender teen, on parents’ support and behavioral intentions regarding their own LGBTQ+ teen. Guided by theories of vicarious contact and inspiring media, we assessed mediation via identification with characters, and via feelings of inspiration and manipulation, testing baseline support as a moderator. Effects of condition were indirect-only, and contingent on baseline support. Among highly supportive parents, growth and acceptance narratives (vs. control) increased feelings of inspiration, which predicted positive behavioral intentions. Among less supportive parents, rejection and (unexpectedly) growth narratives reduced identification with depicted LGBTQ+ teens, indirectly decreasing support and behavioral intentions.

articles.title: The integrative theory of supportive network (re)structuring: a case study in the context of LGBTQ+ hate speech
articles.authors: John P Crowley, Elizabeth A Hintz, Amanda Denes
articles.abstract: Social support is a fundamental human need and communication process. Yet, scholars theorizing about social support have been limited by several pervasive assumptions: (a) people are able to recruit support when needed, (b) others are willing and able to provide support, (c) what counts as “good” support is mutually understood and desirable, and (d) support seeking is binary and static. Researchers must productively move beyond these assumptions to enhance the depth and breadth of theorizing about the process of support seeking. By addressing these assumptions and consolidating the literature concerning support seeking and marshaling, we set forth the novel, field-general integrative theory of supportive network (re)structuring (ITSNS) grounded in the interpretive paradigm. To accomplish this, we introduce process theorizing, forward three propositions forming the ITSNS’ heuristic framework, and offer criteria for evaluating the ITSNS. Finally, to illustrate the utility of the ITSNS in research practice, we offer a case study in the context of LGBTQ+ people seeking support following an experience of hate speech.

articles.title: Examining Children's Language Attitudes Toward Dutch Accents
articles.authors: Stefano De Pascale, Alexander Van Herpe
articles.abstract: Recent studies in developmental sociolinguistics have demonstrated a complex interaction between children's language acquisition, the awareness of linguistic variation and the development of social meaning of language varieties. While Dutch language variation has been extensively studied in attitude research, primarily with adult participants, there is limited knowledge on children's perception of Dutch accents. This study offers a first exploration regarding the development of language attitudes in children, specifically toward what we refer to as Dutch “endogenous” and “exogenous” language varieties. Survey data collected in six primary urban and rural schools in the province of Antwerp, involving 468 six-, eight-, and 11-year-old children, reveal clear patterns. Attitudinal responses concerning solidarity, status, and dynamism vary with children's linguistic and sociocultural background: children in rural schools generally show more positive evaluations of endogenous accents, whereas pupils in urban settings are in comparison more lenient toward exogenous ones.

articles.title: That's Not What I Meant: Assessing Individual Differences in the Perception of Indirect Meaning
articles.authors: Thomas Holtgraves, Rishi Sarin
articles.abstract: The present research developed and evaluated a behavioral measure designed to assess variability in the perception of indirect meaning across multiple pragmatic forms. Three studies were conducted with convenience samples of participants ( N = 453) recruited from either Prolific ( M age = 36.03) or undergraduate research pools ( M age = 18.74). Participants either read or listened to a conversation in English containing 21 utterances instantiating seven types of indirect meaning (e.g., indirect requests, sarcasm, scalar implicatures) and judged the likelihood of indirect interpretations of each. The resulting composite measure demonstrated acceptable internal consistency and person-level reliability when evaluated using variance-partitioning mixed-effects models. Individual differences in indirectness perception were positively associated with multiple indicators of emotional intelligence, including empathy, emotion recognition, and theory of mind, and showed a small but reliable relationship with political ideology. These findings suggest that sensitivity to indirect meaning is a stable individual difference, closely related to social–emotional understanding, and best conceptualized as a composite index of pragmatic inferencing across contexts rather than a unitary latent trait.

articles.title: Enhancing Online Deliberation Through AI-Driven Counter-Attitudinal Interventions: Direct and Indirect Effects on Users’ Perceptions and Behavior
articles.authors: Jana Leonie Peters, Marc Ziegele, Carina Weinmann
articles.abstract: This study tests whether an AI-based counter-attitudinal comment recommender (AI-CAR) enhances participants’ subjective deliberative experiences and reduces incivility by restructuring the visibility of dissenting viewpoints. We analyzed three-wave data from 827 participants in a 10-day simulated digital citizens’ council in Germany. Participants discussed one of two political issues asynchronously and were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: counter-attitudinal AI recommendations, randomly selected recommendations, or no recommendations. Assignment to AI-CAR increased perceived equality of viewpoints. Higher perceived equality at wave 2 was associated with greater internal deliberation and discussion satisfaction at wave 3, controlling for their wave-2 levels. The corresponding model-based indirect effects were statistically significant, whereas comparable indirect effects were not statistically significant for randomly selected recommendations. AI-CAR did not reduce incivility in participants’ contributions. Overall, the findings highlight the potential of AI-driven structural curation to support subjective deliberative experiences, while effects on incivility remain limited.

content.journal_full: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships

articles.title: Transition to Parenthood and Changes in Wellbeing and Relationship Quality: A Propensity Score Matching Approach
articles.authors: Oksana S. Voznyuk, Nickola C. Overall, Chloe Howard, Rachel S. T. Low, Chris G. Sibley
articles.abstract: Does becoming a parent enhance or undermine wellbeing and relationship quality? Mixed findings along with methodological challenges do not provide clear answers. Drawing from nationally representative data in New Zealand collected across 2012–2024, we extended prior studies by using propensity score matching to compare changes in both wellbeing and relationship quality of people who became parents ( n = 1,260) to matched controls who did not become parents ( n = 1,260) but were similar in key socio-demographics and baseline wellbeing and relationship quality. On average, parenthood had small wellbeing benefits. Matched controls experienced small steady declines in life satisfaction and increases in psychological distress. By contrast, people who became parents sustained higher life satisfaction for 2 years following the transition before declining to the same levels as matched controls 4 years later. New parents also did not show increases in psychological distress, but differences to matched controls were small and mostly nonsignificant. Parenthood was also accompanied by relationship challenges. Both matched controls and people who became parents experienced significant declines in relationship satisfaction across time, and these trajectories did not significantly differ. However, new parents reported significantly stronger increases in conflict across the following 4 years compared to matched controls. The results strengthen evidence that parents may experience small life satisfaction benefits, and indicate that declines in relationship satisfaction may not be as unique to the transition to parenthood as prior studies assume, but reveal that new parents may encounter increases in relationship conflict that likely challenge relationship satisfaction and wellbeing.

articles.title: Is Love Gone or Are You Stressed? Examining Daily Associations Between Non-relationship Stress and Love, Passion, and Intimacy in Couple Relationships
articles.authors: Ece Yilmaz, Sarah C. E. Stanton
articles.abstract: Non-relationship stress refers to external stressors that originate outside of the romantic relationship and can include heavy workload, financial problems, conflict with colleagues, and more. Non-relationship stress is related to lower relationship satisfaction; however, other important variables, such as love, passion and intimacy, have not been thoroughly examined in this context. The objective of this preregistered study was to examine the links between daily non-relationship stress and feelings of love, passion, and intimacy. Using a 14-day daily experience dataset of 100 couples, we hypothesized that on days when a person’s (actor effect) and their partner’s (partner effect) non-relational stress is higher (vs. lower), their own love, passion, and intimacy would be lower that day compared to other individuals (between-person effects) and their typical levels (within-person effects). We expected these patterns to hold controlling for daily mood, relationship duration, and prior-day levels of the outcome. However, our confirmatory models revealed that only one’s greater non-relationship stress predicted one’s lower feelings of love, passion, and intimacy. Implications of these results for researchers and professionals working with couples are discussed.

articles.title: Cycling Relationships: An Empirical Typology and its Implications for Relational Functioning
articles.authors: Michael T. Shaw, Xinni Wang, Jordan DiNieri, Maggie M. Parker, Richard E. Mattson
articles.abstract: Cycling relationships are typically defined as committed romantic partnerships that have dissolved and reunited at least once in their history. These couples are relatively common and of growing empirical interest. However, prior research has yielded inconsistent findings about cycling relationships due, in part, to operationalizations that treat them as a homogeneous category, potentially obscuring meaningful variation in how different types of cycling relationships operate. To explore this possibility, the current work applied a two-step cluster analysis to individuals reporting on a current or previous cycling relationship ( n = 261) and compared the emergent groups against each other and to a non-cycling sample ( n = 161) on various relationship and individual characteristics. Three clusters emerged with qualitatively different profiles: A “Deliberate” other-seeking group reported no contact with the cycling partner during long splits wherein they actively sought alternative partnerships. An “Exclusive” cluster evidenced short splits, frequent communication with their cycling partner but without physical intimacy, no other-seeking, and the highest levels of relational certainty. Lastly, a cluster of “Uncertain” other-seekers reported short splits comprising outreaches to alternative partners despite continued sexual intimacy and contact with their cycling partner during splits. This final group had the highest levels of uncertainty and the most dysfunctional relationships. They largely drove observed cycler versus non-cycler differences. Psychological aggression was the only variable that differentiated all three cycling groups from non-cyclers. Our findings suggest that cycling reflects qualitatively distinct relational configurations and that prevailing operationalizations may obscure theoretically consequential heterogeneity within this population.

articles.title: Extending the Deservingness Framework to Communication Sciences
articles.authors: David De Coninck, Lise-Lore Steeman
articles.abstract: While communication research has documented how media frame social groups as victims or threats, little is known about the evaluative criteria through which mediated discourse constructs minority representations. This study introduces deservingness as a framework for analyzing such evaluative logics, drawing on the Control, Attitude, Reciprocity, Identity, Need (CARIN) criteria. We illustrate this through an analysis of 7,561 Belgian newspaper articles across three migration contexts (2015, 2021, 2022), combining automated dictionary-based content analysis with a theory-driven qualitative content analysis of 284 articles. Results reveal a stable but context-sensitive deservingness communication. We position deservingness as a transferable tool for research on moral evaluation and conditional solidarity.

articles.title: Promoting Support for Anti-Racism Movements and Intentions to Intervene: Effects of Common-Identity Narratives and the Moderating Role of Prior Prejudice
articles.authors: Yan Huang, Lan Ni, Zexin Ma, Natasha Saad
articles.abstract: Two experiments examined whether emphasizing a common ingroup identity with racially different characters, operationalized as university affiliation with an African American character (Study 1) and parent identity with an Asian American character (Study 2), enhanced the impact of victim narratives. Findings indicate that emphasizing a common ingroup identity increased perceived similarity and identification with the character and reduced perceived social distance, which then fostered greater support toward anti-racism movements and stronger intentions to intervene. Common-identity narratives were particularly effective among participants with higher prior prejudice, and the moderation effect was mediated by reduced social distance.

articles.title: Perceived Sources Matter: Implications of Misinformation on Media Trust and News Avoidance Under Different Levels of Press Freedom
articles.authors: Yuteng Zheng, Michael Chan, Francis L. F. Lee
articles.abstract: Extant research on the impact of misinformation on media trust and news avoidance behavior has produced competing arguments and findings. The present study argues that the relationships among misinformation, media trust, and news avoidance can be better specified by considering whether people perceive misinformation as coming primarily from established institutions or non-institutional sources. Given the close linkage between the mainstream news media and established social and political institutions, people are likely to exhibit lower levels of news trust and higher levels of news avoidance if they perceive misinformation as coming from institutional sources. In contrast, when people perceive misinformation as coming from non-institutional sources, they may rely on the news media as authoritative fact-checkers and hence trust the news more and avoid it less. Societal-level press freedom is likely to moderate such relationships. The arguments and hypotheses are tested by an analysis of Digital News Report 2025 data.

articles.title: Islamophobia and Online News: Elite News Discourse and Comments About the Daegu Mosque in South Korea
articles.authors: David Chison Oh, Yoon Esther Lee
articles.abstract: In 2023, dozens of Daegu residents protested the construction of a mosque outside of the gates of Kyungpook National University. This article analyzes the discourse of news stories and reader comments in order to understand how the elite news discourse was contested by the popular discourse of a largely far-right comments space. The elite discourse in the newspaper articles normalized institutional authority and the projection of the nation as a liberal democratic actor while the comments articulated common tropes within global Islamophobia while also being grounded in specific local politics and nationalist identity construction set against the Muslim Other.

articles.title: Contested Regimes of (In)Visibility in Gendered Public Spheres
articles.authors: Stefan Wallaschek, Mareike Bauer
articles.abstract: Research on gendered public spheres has examined how struggles over gender equality, recognition, and equal representation unfold across changing communication environments. These struggles involve competing actors and claims, including feminist and queer mobilization as well as anti-gender contestation, but they are also shaped by how and under what conditions actors become visible, remain less visible, or strategically manage their public exposure. This thematic issue conceptualizes gendered public spheres as contested regimes of (in)visibility and brings together contributions that address three closely connected dimensions: the structural conditions that shape visibility; the situated agency through which actors navigate them; and the relational production of visibility across networks, publics, and national boundaries. Together, the contributions show that visibility is neither inherently empowering nor always the desired outcome, while invisibility cannot simply be equated with exclusion or political irrelevance. The thematic issue contributes to research on feminist and anti-gender mobilization, platformized and networked publics, strategic (in)visibility, and the relationship between visibility and influence in contemporary gendered public spheres.

articles.title: Hashtag Wars: Analysing “Digital Woyane” and “Digital Media Army” During the War on Tigray
articles.authors: Hagos Nigussie, Hagos Sibhat, Gebru Kiflu
articles.abstract: The Ethiopian government declared war on Tigray (2020–2022) amid the country’s ethno-polarised political landscape and state-imposed communications shutdown, emphasising the strategic importance of Twitter (now X) for narrative control, mobilisation, and international influence. This study examines the hashtag campaigns of the pro-Tigray Digital Woyane and the Ethiopian government-aligned Digital Media Army. It conceptualises hashtag activism as a form of information warfare in which strategic narratives seek to establish legitimacy, mobilise supporters, and delegitimise adversaries. Guided by social identity theory, this study employed a mixed-methods design involving quantitative content analysis and critical discourse analysis of tweets and hashtags, supplemented by manual screenshot collection (<em>n</em> = 500). The findings show that Digital Woyane (252 tweets) primarily highlighted civilian suffering through narratives of atrocities, hunger, humanitarian crises (including the killing of Médecins Sans Frontières staff), and appeals to international institutions before progressively shifting towards themes of resistance. In contrast, the Digital Media Army (248 tweets) emphasised sovereignty, national unity, and denial narratives while systematically delegitimising and discrediting international media and reports of human rights violations. Overall, the hashtag campaigns functioned as a form of information warfare, facilitating transnational advocacy while simultaneously amplifying propaganda and competing narratives on X. This study contributes to our understanding of how X shapes conflict narratives, amplifies selective information, and reinforces information warfare in contemporary armed conflicts.

articles.title: Transnationalization of Anti-Gender Politics on Social Media: Hashtag Practices and Cross-Border Visibility
articles.authors: Dominika Tronina
articles.abstract: Gender politics have become central arenas of contemporary political struggle, with anti-gender movements mobilizing across borders to contest women’s and LGBTQI+ rights. While research has shown that anti-gender actors articulate strikingly similar positions across national contexts, it remains insufficiently understood how such similarity translates into shared transnational action. This study examines how anti-gender movements collectively generate transnational visibility on social media by analyzing ten years of Twitter (now X) communication from 148 anti-gender social movement organizations in Croatia, Germany, France, Italy, and Poland (<em>N</em> = 126,711 tweets). Drawing on concepts of networked framing and discourse coalitions, this study employs a mixed-methods analysis of hashtag co-usage on Twitter, combining quantitative measures of transnational hashtag connectivity with qualitative thematic content analysis. The findings reveal that anti-gender movements co-create visibility for opposition to gender equality through a threefold pattern, including a continuous dissemination of ideological narratives, an episodic activation of campaigns, and a strategic extension of anti-gender frames into broader public debates. These practices enable actors to jointly enhance the visibility and persistence of anti-gender claims across multiple publics while simultaneously adapting frames to divergent political contexts. By linking cross-border hashtag practices to the co-production of visibility, this study contributes to research on gendered public spheres by demonstrating how similarity among anti-gender actors becomes transnationally consequential through the joint production of visibility in networked communication environments.

articles.title: Between Trans Solidarity and Trans-Antagonism: Affective Contestations Around Germany’s Self-Determination Act on TikTok
articles.authors: Annabella Backes, Ana Makhashvili, Andrea Lora Rojas
articles.abstract: <p>This article examines affective contestations surrounding Germany’s Self-Determination Act on TikTok. Drawing on a mixed-methods design combining hashtag co-occurrence analysis with qualitative multimodal analysis, the study investigates which emotions become publicly visible, legitimized, and contested in struggles over gender recognition, and how they are (re)produced through different affective registers. The analysis is based on a dataset of 1,509 TikTok videos collected between May 2023 and November 2025 using the hashtags #sbgg and #selbstbestimmungsgesetz. The findings show that the debate is organized through competing affective-discursive formations. Trans-affirming creators mobilize care, solidarity, moderated anger, cautious relief, and structurally grounded fear to render visible the everyday burdens of legal misrecognition and the partial relief offered by administrative self-determination. Trans-antagonistic and far-right actors, by contrast, construct the law as a threat to cis women, children, anti-trans speakers, and social order, redistributing vulnerability away from trans people and attaching danger to trans women’s bodily presence and legal recognition, and imagining future harms. Building on these findings, the article argues that platformized gender politics are organized through struggles over whose vulnerability becomes publicly legible, whose emotions appear credible, and whose recognition is made to feel either necessary or dangerous.</p>

articles.title: The Governance of Queer Visibility in Platformized Public Spheres
articles.authors: Irina Bănoiu, Laura Wiesböck
articles.abstract: Queer visibility in contemporary digital cultures is increasingly mediated by platformized public spheres, where it is both produced and governed through socio-technical infrastructures. While social media platforms provide important opportunities for queer users—including community formation, identity exploration, and circulation of counternarratives beyond traditional gatekeeping institutions—they simultaneously organize visibility in uneven ways. Platform infrastructures embed normative assumptions and capitalistic incentives that selectively amplify, suppress, or modulate queer expression through mechanisms of datafication, selection, and commodification. As a result, queer visibility is a structurally precarious condition marked by the simultaneous presence of hypervisibility, erasure, and surveillance. Bringing critical platform studies and social justice theory into dialogue, this conceptual article analyses how new regimes of queer visibility emerge and are shaped by platform mechanisms and considers their implications for representation, recognition, and redistribution. In doing so, it develops an analytical framework centered on three interlocking governance logics—quantification, normativity, and profitability—that organize visibility as a site of contestation and an object of control. Finally, the article introduces the concept of “platformized (in)visibilization” to describe the ambivalent role of platforms as both enabling and constraining environments for expression in contemporary digital cultures, affecting political legitimacy, social equality, and economic justice.

articles.title: Does Algorithmic Personalization Make Us Happier? The Effects of Algorithmic (Dis)connection on Digital Well‑Being
articles.authors: Xin Liu, Kejing Guo, Wenqing Cheng, Siyue Li

articles.title: Cosmopolitan Sonic Intimacies: Listening as Civic Infrastructure in Diasporic Mobile Media
articles.authors: Tharupathi Munasinghe
articles.abstract: Mobile media scholarship has extensively theorised textual and visual intimacies, yet sound remains underexamined as a modality through which migrants sustain transnational belonging. This article develops an account of sonic intimacy —forms of connection mediated through voice, music, and acoustic atmosphere via mobile platforms—and argues that recurrent listening practices operate as civic infrastructure in diasporic life. It builds on Malcolm James's analysis of sonic intimacy in Black British diasporic sound cultures and extends Pertierra's concept of discursive intimacy, situating both within mobile sound and mobile messaging research. Drawing on sonic ethnographic research with Sri Lankan migrant communities in Melbourne, including 30 interviews, participant sound recordings, and platform artefact analysis, the article examines listening across political mobilisation, religious ritual, and everyday mobile use. WhatsApp voice messages, YouTube temple archives, and TikTok remixes are shown to sustain recognition, belonging, participation, and audibility—the four dimensions through which listening becomes infrastructural. Cosmopolitan sonic intimacy emerges as an outcome of these practices rather than a competing framework: Migrants from CALD backgrounds cultivate cosmopolitan sensibilities through everyday listening practices rather than elite consumption. The article contributes to mobile media scholarship by demonstrating that sound operates as a primary rather than supplementary modality of platform-mediated intimacy and that attending to it reveals dimensions of mobile life invisible to text-focused analysis.

articles.title: Practicing love with algorithms: How online communities narrate and make sense of human–AI intimacy
articles.authors: Fanjue Liu, Haiyan Hao, Kun Xu
articles.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes embedded in everyday life, emotionally intimate interactions with AI companions are becoming increasingly visible. Yet prior research has focused mainly on individual experiences, leaving limited understanding of how human–AI intimacy is collectively interpreted and negotiated in online communities. This study examines community discourse on RedNote, a major Chinese social and lifestyle platform, using 13,059 comments from 58 relevant posts. Combining BERTopic modeling with a human–large language model (LLM) hybrid emotion classification procedure, the analysis identifies three thematic clusters: intimacy as co-construction, intimacy as infrastructure, and intimacy as boundary negotiation. Co-construction centers on persona design, roleplay, and narrative world-building and is marked mainly by joy and curiosity. Infrastructure-related discourse is associated with frustration and sadness, while boundary negotiation reflects ambivalence toward intimacy with AI.

articles.title: Affluence without status: Classed meanings of working-class leisure activities on the Finnish-language Internet
articles.authors: Mikael Wallin
articles.abstract: Previous research suggests that working-class culture is underrepresented or stigmatised, particularly in commercial and digital media environments shaped by middle-class values. Using a two-phase research design, this study investigates how working-class lifestyles are represented in Finnish-language Internet discourse through the semantic associations of leisure activities. In the first phase, via nationally representative survey data, I identify leisure activities that are disproportionately characteristic of working-class occupational groups. In the second phase, a word-embedding model trained on a large dataset representing the Finnish-language Internet is used to examine how these activities align with class-related semantic dimensions. The results indicate that working-class leisure activities are positively associated with affluence, cultural cultivation, and moral legitimacy and negatively associated with social status, while only weakly associated with education, workplace position, and gender. These findings suggest that working-class culture remains institutionally marginalised despite connotations of legitimacy and affluence.

articles.title: Dyadic Trajectories of Financial Behaviors in Marriage: Predictors, Consequences, and Structural Disparities
articles.authors: Xiaomin Li, Dexia Kong, Muhammad Aamir Khan, Heather Kelley, Jeremy Yorgason
articles.abstract: This study investigates the joint developmental trajectories of financial behaviors, their predictors, and outcomes within the first decade of marriage. We used Waves 2–7 (six waves) of dyadic data from 1505 different‐gender couples. Growth curve analyses showed that healthy financial behaviors continued to increase but began declining between Wave 5 (April 2021–December 2021) and Wave 6 (April 2022–December 2022), coinciding with economic challenges at the time. Latent profile analyses identified three subgroups: “moderate momenta with fades” (P1, 40.3%), “peaking and ebbing” (P2, 36.3%), and “stalling in shallows” (P3, 23.5%). P1 and P2 were associated with higher relational commitment than P3. Socioeconomic inequalities were the key predictors. Higher education and household income were associated with higher likelihoods of the more adaptive P1 and P2 (compared to P3). Wives' longer working hours and husbands' prior marriage were linked to a lower likelihood of P2 than P3. P2 was more likely (than P1) when household income and wives' education were higher, but less likely when wives worked longer hours or husbands had a prior marriage. Our study advances family finance research by demonstrating how couples' financial behaviors co‐evolve and highlights the urgent need for financial interventions, particularly among socioeconomically marginalized populations.

articles.title: Dyadic Influences of Affect and Depth of Cognitive Processing on How Empathic Expressions Are Perceived in Supportive Interactions
articles.authors: Nhung C. Vu, Andrew C. High
articles.abstract: Communicating empathy in supportive interactions can be an effective way for providers to help regulate receivers' emotions. Partners' perceptions of empathic expressions can be influenced by various factors, including the affect they bring into an interaction and the extent to which they engage in cognitive processing. Drawing on the affect infusion model (AIM) and the emotion as social information (EASI) model, this study examined the influence of incidental affect on perceptions of empathic expressions and how this influence is moderated by the depth of partners' cognitive processing regarding a conversation. Partners in established relationships reported their affect before an interaction, were randomly assigned to be either support providers or receivers, engaged in a supportive interaction, and then reported their level of cognitive processing and perceptions of the providers' empathic expressions. Individuals' positive affect positively influenced their own, but not their partner's perceptions of empathic expressions. How deeply participants engaged in cognitive processing moderated the influence of their affect on their perceptions of providers' empathic expressions.

articles.title: Understanding how exposure to science content on social media shapes normative expectations of scientists’ communication: A social media affordances perspective
articles.authors: Annie Li Zhang
articles.abstract: As social media continue to shape where science is communicated and how it is consumed, this study adopts an affordances approach to advance our understanding of how audiences observe and make sense of online scientific content and evaluate science and scientists more broadly. By analyzing a two-wave survey ( N = 878) conducted in February and March 2025, this study reveals that online science content exposure is associated with increased normative expectations across a range of scientists’ communication behaviors, including political advocacy, warmth- and competence-oriented strategies, and public engagement. In addition, stronger expectations of competency-oriented communication and political advocacy were associated with greater trust in and vulnerability toward scientists. Political ideology was found to moderate the relationship between science observation and certain normative expectations. Findings underscore the role of social media in influencing science communication norms and (re)shaping what it means to be a trustworthy scientist in an increasingly visible and networked media environment.

articles.title: Communication and science mediation services in French universities and research centers: When institutional reconfigurations become a way of asserting professional identity
articles.authors: Nicolas Brard, Elsa Poupardin
articles.abstract: This article examines how communication and science mediation services in French universities and research centers organize the public communication of science and how institutional reconfigurations affect professional identities. Based on 31 semi-structured interviews and a complementary questionnaire (n = 57) conducted in 2025, it analyzes how professionals define their roles, negotiate relationships with researchers and governance bodies, and interpret changes linked to funding, reporting, participation-oriented policies, and institutional visibility. The findings show that communication and science mediation are not merely different tasks but distinct professional identity orientations, grounded in different trajectories, values, methods, relationships to publics, and forms of legitimacy. Reconfigurations are often perceived less as a participatory turn than as processes of renaming, reporting, and adjustment. Finally, instability is incorporated differently into professional identities: communicators present adaptation as a core expertise, whereas science mediation professionals more often experience reconfigurations as threatening the specificity and public-service orientation of their work.

articles.title: Conflict With Context: The Impact of Explanations of Scientific Uncertainty and Informant Differences on Responses to Conflicting Health Advice
articles.authors: Yanmengqian Zhou, Youzhen Su
articles.abstract: This experiment examined whether conflict explanations (informant-based, uncertainty-based, vs. none) and conflict framing (alternative vs. opposing) mitigate negative responses to conflicting health advice. Both explanations reduced perceived conflict, with informant-based explanations effective only among individuals with lower perceived knowledge. No significant effect of conflict framing was observed. Perceived conflict was subsequently associated with greater confusion, uncertainty, anger, and anxiety. Uncertainty, in turn, was more strongly associated with topic-specific attitude ambivalence, whereas anger was more strongly associated with generalized health confusion and backlash. Mediation analysis further supported several indirect effects of conflict explanations on downstream outcomes through these pathways.

articles.title: Do Experts Agree About Misinformation? Evidence From Three Annual Surveys
articles.authors: Sacha Altay, Sebastián Valenzuela, Philip N. Howard
articles.abstract: How much do experts on the information environment agree about the scale, spread, and effects of misinformation? We drew on three annual waves of the International Panel on the Information Environment expert survey to examine agreement with seven popular claims about misinformation (2023: N = 262; 2024: N = 413; 2025: N = 442; spanning 76 countries). Agreement varied widely across statements and was stable across waves. About 60% of experts agreed that falsehoods spread faster than the truth and that misinformation is widespread. About half agreed that misinformation has a substantial influence on behavior and that people readily believe what they see online; about 40% agreed that more people have become misinformed over time; and only 25% agreed that misinformation is primarily a social media problem. The surveys also revealed a persistent divide between experts who saw misinformation as widespread and consequential and those more skeptical, with sharpest disagreement on its behavioral impact and increase over time. In 2025, some experts distinguished between misperception prevalence and misinformation severity. Overall agreement varied by respondent background: agreement was higher among experts on developing countries than those on developed countries, higher among STEM researchers than social scientists, and lower among political scientists than communication scholars. Expert consensus on misinformation is partial, varies across claims and experts, and is shaped by geography and discipline.

articles.title: Exploring the Predictors and Outcomes of Perceived Algorithm Responsiveness in Social Media Feeds: Combining Longitudinal and Computational Methods
articles.authors: Samuel Hardman Taylor, David M. Markowitz
articles.abstract: Perceptions of how algorithms curate content are integral to how people use social media and its effects. Building on the algorithm responsiveness process, we explore whether perceived algorithm responsiveness (PAR) was associated with the message cues of algorithmically curated content. We coupled longitudinal data from a 7-day, twice-daily diary survey with computational digital traces from Twitter (now X) to operationalize algorithmic message characteristics and to understand the antecedents and outcomes of PAR ( N = 10,337 tweets). Results suggested that message cues from algorithmic content in social feeds (i.e., closeness, popularity, valence, and format) were associated with perceived message personalization, but message personalization was the only message characteristic associated with PAR. PAR predicted feeling more connected to others on Twitter, along with message-level factors: closeness to the poster and message personalization. This work contributes to the algorithm responsiveness process, demonstrating that characteristics of algorithmically curated messages predict how individuals experience algorithms.

articles.title: Cross-channel users' hostile expression on YouTube: Evidence from digital trace data
articles.authors: Han Lin, Bumsoo Kim

articles.title: Deceit between Falshoods and Morality: Unpacking Audience Engagement with Disinformation
articles.authors: Sabina Mihelj, Stefan Janjić, Hanna Orsolya Vincze, Andreea Alina Mogoş
articles.abstract: Disinformation is customarily approached through an epistemic lens and defined with reference to intentionally false or misleading information. Yet, this approach struggles to account for how disinformation functions as a communicative practice that acquires meaning through audience interpretation and interaction. To develop a more comprehensive understanding, we draw on the analysis of eighteen focus groups conducted in 2025 in three countries that have been under increased scrutiny internationally due to their vulnerability to pro-Russian disinformation, but received limited attention in existing research: Poland, Romania and Serbia. Focusing on responses to examples of pro-Russian disinformation concerning the Russia-Ukraine war and LGBTQ+ rights, we show that participants judged claims not only based on credibility but also based on moral rightness, as well as engaged in contestations over the boundaries of legitimate controversy. Building on this evidence, we argue that disinformation not only creates uncertainty over how the world is but often invites contestation over how the world should be and over where the boundaries of legitimate public debate should lie. We conclude by reflecting on what these findings mean for scholarly research on disinformation, for counter-disinformation efforts, and for the way we understand the impact of disinformation on democracy.

articles.title: Visualizing resilience in crowdfunding: rhetoric of vulnerable and promotional actors during the COVID-19 pandemic and the Russia–Ukraine war
articles.authors: Maria Eronen-Valli, Virpi Salojärvi
articles.abstract: This study explores how two mega-crises – the COVID-19 pandemic and the Russia–Ukraine war – are portrayed in photographic performances of resilience in crowdfunding campaign calls of small companies. These companies, aside from being commercial actors, are organizations consisting of individual crisis experiencers and eyewitnesses. The authors examine 234 photographic visuals (168 photographs, 43 photo collages, 21 GIFs and 2 GIF collages) in 53 crisis-related crowdfunding campaign calls (19 Finnish, 18 North American, and 16 Ukrainian) on three different platforms. The data are analysed with a focus on visual rhetoric. The study contributes to previous visual analyses by finding five visually performed connotations of resilience: suffering, endurance, resistance, peer support and hope. The article concludes that, in the era of mega-crises, crowdfunding has become a merged discursive site for both promotional and testimonial performances, varying from a private to communal focus and thereby involving both business-related and societal functions.
